newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says domestic ice-cream in league of its own.
newsitem.headline: Russia says domestic ice-cream in league of its own.

text.p: Russia's ice-cream producers defended their own cones and wafers against flashy imports on Wednesday and said they were confident the future looked sweet.

"Russian products, whatever anyone says, always have been and always will be of a high quality...How can you compare Western ice-cream with domestic ice-cream?" said Olga Yevseyeva, general director of Moscow's Servis-Kholod ice-cream plant.

Gathered to present new product lines for Moscow's 850th anniversary this year, the heads of several Moscow-based ice-cream factories shrugged off the threat from exotic Western brands, saying Russians were ice-cream patriots at heart.
"We know that people like our ice cream -- it's got a Russian flavour, our flavour," said Evseyeva.

Like much of Russian industry, Russia's ice-cream producers have been hit hard by economic reforms. Output has plummeted to 181,400 tonnes in 1996 from 350,000 tonnes in 1990, the year before reforms began, according to some industry figures.

Brightly-packaged and multi-flavoured imports have flooded into the market since the beginning of economic reforms, while Western ice-cream producers, including Ben & Jerry's, Baskin-Robbins and Nestle, have invested in Russian production.

But producers said foreign imports were now declining, making up only 12 percent of the Russian ice-cream market in 1996, and attributed the return to favour of the more dowdily-packaged Russian brands to their relatively value.

"Take a box of sweets, with a huge label -- open it up and there's only two or three sweets in there," said Yevseyeva. "We have a thin little label, but open it up and there's 100 grammes of ice-cream."
President Boris Yeltsin called last month for Russian consumers to "buy Russian" in a show of support for struggling domestic producers.
But the ice-cream magnates said their main problems were debts between enterprises and high energy and water costs, and called for the reduction of a 20 percent government "delicacy" sales tax.

"We producers don't understand why this food category, which is produced completely out of dairy products, is classified as a delicacy," said Anatoly Shamanov, general director of Ice-Fili ice-cream factory.
Many Russians trying to eke out a living on meagre salaries can no longer afford to treat themselves to ice cream.

Alexander Klady, an ice-cream expert and author of a history of ice-cream, says per capita ice-cream consumption fell to 1.5 kilogrammes a year in 1996 compared to 3.5 kilogrammes in 1987 and an average 10 to 15 kilogrammes a year in the United States.

He says Russians have had a soft spot for ice-cream since sweetened curds were frozen in the snow during pre-Lent festivals. According to another story, Peter the Great brought ice-cream back from France in the 17th century.
Ice-cream was a delicacy reserved for the noble classes in tsarist Russia and became mass-produced only after the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.

"It was considered abnormal to go to the theatre or cinema and not eat ice cream and it was sold in all the big stores. But it was always vanilla, there was very little chocolate," said Baskin-Robbins marketing manager Darya Kaplunova.
Even now, ice-cream sellers seem as numerous in winter's sub-zero temperatures as in the summer.
"Russians eat even more in winter, although it sounds strange," said Kaplunova. "Perhaps it's because in summer it melts by the time you get it home. In winter you can eat it as long as you want."
